scene.testo: You are moving at 17,500 miles per hour. Right now. While you read this, you would circle the entire Earth in about 90 minutes. That's the speed of the International Space Station, and the people inside it still have to get up for work.

Imagine you are floating in the station at 6 AM. No alarm clock rings in your ear. A sleeping bag is strapped to the wall of a closet-sized room, and you are drifting inside it. There is no up. There is no down.

Here is what you probably picture. Astronauts floating around, laughing, flipping through the air all day. The truth is far busier. Their day is planned almost minute by minute, by teams of people on the ground.

The station orbits about 250 miles above Earth. That's roughly the distance from New York City to Washington, D.C., except straight up. And here's the part that breaks most people's brains. You never fall to the ground.

Why? Because you are falling all the time. The station falls toward Earth, but it moves sideways so fast that the ground curves away beneath it. You miss the planet again and again. That is what orbit really means.

Gravity is still there. At that height, it is about 90 percent as strong as on the ground. You feel weightless only because everything around you falls together. You, the walls, your toothbrush, your breakfast.

So how do you sleep? You zip into that bag and tie it down. If you didn't, you would drift into a fan or a wall. Your arms float up in front of you. Many astronauts say it feels like sleeping on a cloud.

Then the day begins. Your crew wakes up on a set schedule, usually in Greenwich Mean Time. Why? Because the station sees a sunrise or a sunset roughly every 45 minutes. The sun cannot tell you when it's morning.

That's right. Sixteen sunrises and sixteen sunsets every single day. Each one lasts only moments. Gold light, then blue, then black. Astronauts have described the view as the one thing they never get tired of.

Before breakfast, there's a morning routine. You brush your teeth, but you can't spit into a sink. You swallow the toothpaste, or you wipe your mouth with a towel. It's the first lesson of space: everything floats.

Washing your hair works differently too. You squeeze a little water onto your head and use no-rinse shampoo. The water clings to your skin like a layer of jelly. Then you towel it off. There are no showers on the station.

Now, breakfast. Your food comes in sealed pouches and cans, made on Earth and sent up on cargo ships. Cereal, scrambled eggs, fruit, coffee. You add water through a small needle, because the meal is often dried.

Crumbs are the enemy. A loose crumb floats off and can end up in a filter or someone's eye. So tortillas replace bread on the station. Salt and pepper come as liquids, because floating grains could clog the equipment.

Even your coffee is a puzzle. Drinks float in blobs, so astronauts sip from pouches with straws. A special cup was designed for the station that uses the shape of its walls to pull the liquid toward your mouth.

After breakfast, the crew holds a daily check-in with mission control. Teams in Houston and other centers read out the plan. Today's experiments, today's repairs, today's visitors. Then the real work begins.

And the real work is science. The station is a laboratory with six research labs worth of equipment. Astronauts study how plants grow, how flames burn, how fluids behave, how the human body changes in space.

Fire behaves differently up there. Without gravity, a candle flame turns into a tiny blue ball. That strange behavior helps engineers design better engines and safer fire detectors, here on the ground.

Some days, you grow food. Crews on the station have grown lettuce, radishes, and chili peppers, using special lights and a small growing system. In 2015, astronauts ate lettuce they had grown themselves, a first for NASA.

Other days, you work on your own body. Because without gravity, muscles and bones weaken. Astronauts can lose bone density at a rate of about 1 percent per month, according to NASA. That's why exercise is not optional.

Two hours every day. That's the standard NASA exercise plan. You run on a treadmill while strapped in with a harness. You lift weights using a vacuum-powered machine. You pedal a bike that is bolted to the floor.

Sweat doesn't drip. It clings to your skin and forms a bead. Then it floats away from you in the air. The station's air system catches it, and then something remarkable happens. The water is recycled.

Yes, you read that right. The station recycles sweat, breath moisture, and even urine into drinking water. NASA says the system recovers about 98 percent of the water on board. Coffee made from yesterday's coffee, in a way.

Next, lunch. And then, afternoon work. This is when you might fix something. The station is as long as a football field, including its solar panels, and something is always breaking. A pump, a filter, a toilet.

The toilet is a big deal. It uses airflow, not water, to pull waste away from your body. You strap your feet down and use a seat belt on your legs. Get it wrong, and the problem floats. Everyone remembers their first try.
Some afternoons, though, the work is outside. A spacewalk. You put on a suit that weighs about 300 pounds on Earth. It is a tiny spaceship you wear, with its own air, water, cooling, and radio.

Outside, the temperature swings are brutal. In sunlight, surfaces can reach about +250°F. In shadow, they can fall to about -250°F. That's a swing of 500 degrees, every 45 minutes, as the station circles Earth.

A spacewalk can last about six to seven hours. Your hands tire first. The gloves are stiff, like squeezing a tennis ball all day. Astronauts say their fingertips get sore from pushing against the glove walls.

Before every spacewalk, you breathe pure oxygen for hours. Why? To flush nitrogen out of your blood. Without that step, the lower pressure in the suit could cause decompression sickness, the same thing divers call the bends.

Then you float out the hatch. Below your boots, Earth rolls by at 17,500 miles an hour. You are tied to the station by a tether. Lose that line, and you have a small jet pack as a backup, called SAFER.

After the workday, there's dinner. And this is the best part of the day for many crews. Everyone gathers at the table, strapped in or floating, sharing meals from many countries. Americans, Russians, Europeans, Japanese, Canadians.

The menu has about 200 items, according to NASA. Shrimp cocktail is a favorite. Why shrimp cocktail? Astronauts say the spicy horseradish sauce helps, because in space, your nose gets stuffy and food tastes blander.

On weekends, the pace slows down. Crews still clean, still exercise, but they also get free time. They call family on video, take photographs of Earth, watch movies, play music, or just stare out the window.
The Cupola is the best window on the station. It has seven panes, and the largest is about 31 inches wide. From there, you can watch storms, cities at night, and lightning flashing under the clouds.

Now compare it with your day. Your commute? A few minutes, or an hour in traffic. Theirs? Zero. They live at work. They sleep at work. And they can't just walk outside for fresh air when they need a break.

The living space is about the size of a six-bedroom house, NASA says. But it's packed with machines, and much of it is off limits to sleeping. For months at a time, you share it with the same few people.

Then there's the noise. The station hums with fans and pumps, day and night. Astronauts often wear earplugs to sleep. It's one reason crews describe a strange feeling when they return, hearing silence for the first time.

And then there's the goodbye. At the end of a mission, the crew climbs into a capsule, such as a Soyuz. The ride home starts with a burn, and then the capsule hits the atmosphere at about 17,500 miles an hour.

Outside the window, fire glows around the capsule. The heat shield faces temperatures of thousands of degrees. Then parachutes open, and the capsule drifts down into the grasslands of Kazakhstan, where rescue teams are waiting.

And here is the surprising part. After months in orbit, your legs feel like lead. Standing up is hard. Many astronauts get dizzy. Your body forgot gravity, and you have to learn all over again to walk, balance, and carry yourself.

So what do astronauts do all day? They fix, they test, they exercise, they eat, they sleep tied to a wall. They live a life that is part laboratory, part repair shop, part tiny town, 250 miles above all of us.

And the most surprising detail? The crew has been living up there nonstop since November 2, 2000. For years, humans have never left. Right now, as you watch this, people are floating above your head, doing their chores.

descrizione:
What do astronauts actually do all day? Step inside the International Space Station and follow a real day in orbit: waking up in a sleeping bag, eating from pouches, exercising two hours to protect your bones, doing science, fixing equipment, and floating out on a spacewalk at +250°F and -250°F.

Learn how the station travels at 17,500 mph about 250 miles above Earth, why astronauts see 16 sunrises every day, how the water recycling system recovers about 98 percent of the water on board, and what the return to Earth really feels like.

All facts come from NASA, ESA, and astronauts' own accounts, and all footage is real NASA archive video. Subscribe to Orbital Days for more daily life in space.
